turns.content: I don't understand how a gas turbine engine is different from a piston engine if they're both internal combustion engines.

Both are internal combustion engines sharing the same cycle: induction, compression, combustion, expansion, and exhaust. The key difference is timing. In a piston engine, each of these events occurs as a separate, distinct occurrence in each cylinder, one cycle at a time, with an ignition event during each cycle. In a gas turbine engine, all these phases occur simultaneously and continuously rather than successively. Also, ignition in a gas turbine only occurs during the starting cycle and is continuous thereafter, not repeated each cycle.

turns.content: For my checkride, how would I explain the starting sequence of a gas turbine engine?

To start a gas turbine engine, an electric starter normally rotates the compressor section. As compressor rpm increases, air flowing through the inlet is compressed to high pressure and delivered to the combustion section where it is ignited. Once the hot gases from the burner section provide sufficient power to maintain engine operation through the turbine, the starter is de-energized and the starting sequence ends. Combustion then continues until the engine is shut down by cutting off the fuel supply.

turns.content: Why doesn't all the compressed air go into the combustion chamber? What happens to the rest of it?

Not all compressed air is used to support combustion. Some of the compressed air bypasses the burner section within the engine to provide internal cooling. This bypass air later mixes with the very hot combustion gases, which exit the burner at around 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit, dropping the mixed air temperature down to a range of 1,600 to 2,400 degrees Fahrenheit before it passes through the turbine blades.

The turbine drives the compressor section by means of a direct shaft, a concentric shaft, or a combination of both. The turbine is powered by the expanding mixture of hot combustion gases and bypass air flowing through the turbine blades, and that rotational energy is transferred back to keep the compressor spinning.

The fuel and air mixture in the combustion chamber burns at approximately 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit. turns.content: What exactly is bleed air and what is it used for?

Bleed air is hot compressed air tapped from the engine compressor. Because compression produces both heat and pressure, this air can be extracted and used for several aircraft systems after further conditioning its internal pressure and temperature. Uses include engine anti-ice, airfoil anti-ice, aircraft pressurization, and other ancillary systems.

turns.content: I'm not sure why transitioning to a turboprop requires so much extra training beyond just learning the new airplane systems. Can you explain?

Turboprop airplanes operate in medium and high altitudes that present an entirely different environment compared to lower-altitude piston flying. That environment involves different regulatory requirements, a different airspace structure, unique physiological demands on the pilot, and different meteorological conditions. Because of all these factors, transition training must go well beyond just learning new systems. Ground training needs to cover the flight environment, weather, flight planning and navigation, physiological aspects of high-altitude flight, oxygen and pressurization system operation, and high-altitude emergencies. It is a comprehensive change in operating environment, not just a change in aircraft type.
